cards.claim: Candidate chose not to build the obvious thing — a candidate-assessment tool — and instead picked a real, concrete pain point (client onboarding intake) with clear reasons for why AI adds value there.

citation.quote: I considered building an assessment tool, but I kept returning to what the job description actually rewards: finding a real pain point inside an ambiguous enterprise context and shipping a workflow that respects governance.

refutation.rationale: The write-up contains the exact quote and the reasoning is spelled out clearly — the candidate explains the choice in terms of what the role rewards. Nothing elsewhere in the submission contradicts this.

cards.claim: Candidate named a specific, measurable cost to justify the problem — coordinators spending 25 to 40 minutes re-keying data per client, with errors showing up weeks later.

citation.quote: Coordinators told me the re-keying alone takes 25 to 40 minutes per client and errors surface weeks later as billing and conflict-check problems.

refutation.rationale: The quote is present verbatim and the numbers (25–40 minutes, errors surfacing weeks later) are stated as direct feedback from coordinators. No other document contradicts them.

cards.claim: Candidate clearly described which parts of the work are a good fit for automation (repetitive, rule-bound middle steps) and which are not (judgment calls at the edges).

citation.quote: The workflow is repetitive, rule-bound, and full of judgment calls at the edges — exactly the shape where an agent helps with the middle and humans must own the edges.

refutation.rationale: The quote supports the claim. The write-up distinguishes the repetitive middle (agent-suitable) from edge judgment calls (human-owned), and the workflow structure backs this up.

cards.claim: The workflow has an explicit human review step before any extracted data can enter the CRM — the AI output is never written to the record of truth without a person checking it first.

citation.quote: A human reviews every extracted client profile before it enters the CRM — extraction is allowed to be wrong; the record of truth is not.

refutation.rationale: The write-up says a human reviews every extracted profile before it enters the CRM, but the actual workflow connects 'Validate required fields' directly to 'Create CRM record' with no human-review node in between. There is no approval or hold step anywhere in the workflow export.

cards.claim: Before building, candidate wrote down which steps the agent owns and which it can never reach — conflict checks, fee arrangements, and ledger writes are blocked by the structure of the workflow, not just by a prompt instruction.

citation.quote: I wrote down, before building, which steps the agent owns and which it never will... those stay human, and the workflow is built so they cannot be reached from the automated path.

refutation.rationale: The write-up describes the pre-build decision, and the workflow's connection map confirms that conflict checks, fee arrangements, and ledger writes have no nodes and no paths leading to them — they are simply absent from the automated path.

cards.claim: The workflow shows a clearly built failure path: when validation fails, records go to an exceptions channel with original documents attached rather than being dropped silently.

citation.quote: "Exceptions: route to review": { "type": "n8n-nodes-base.slack", "parameters": { "channel": "#onboarding-exceptions", "text": "Validation failed: {{$json.missing_fields}} — original documents attached." } }

refutation.rationale: The exceptions node exists in the workflow export with the exact channel name and message text shown in the quote. The claim is directly demonstrated by the workflow structure.

cards.claim: The demo shows live that the restricted steps (conflict checks and fee arrangements) are structurally unreachable from the automated path — not just mentioned in a prompt.

citation.quote: The parts I didn't automate — conflict checks and fee arrangements — aren't reachable from this path at all, which I think matters more than any prompt instruction.

refutation.rationale: The transcript quote is present and the workflow export confirms that conflict checks and fee arrangements have no nodes at all — they genuinely cannot be reached from the automated path.

cards.claim: A runnable n8n workflow export exists, covering the full path from a new intake submission through parsing, AI extraction, validation, CRM record creation, and team notification.

refutation.rationale: The workflow export shows all the named nodes — webhook intake, parse attachments, Claude extraction, field validation, CRM record creation — connected in the right order. The full path is present.

cards.claim: The demo video shows the workflow actually running end to end — webhook fires, Claude returns a structured profile, CRM record is created, and the Slack notification appears.

citation.quote: The webhook fires, attachments get parsed, and here's the Claude extraction node returning the structured profile. Notice jurisdiction came back as Ontario and entity type as corporation — both correct for this fixture.

refutation.rationale: The transcript describes what the candidate says is happening on screen, but the transcript alone cannot confirm the workflow actually ran live. We can read the narration but cannot see the video or verify that outputs were real rather than staged.

cards.claim: The extraction prompt is specific enough for someone else to pick up and run — it names exact output fields, requires JSON only, and tells the model not to guess missing values.

citation.quote: "prompt": "Extract a structured client profile from the intake text: legal_name, jurisdiction, entity_type, engagement_type, key_contacts[]. Return JSON only. If a required field is missing, set it to null — do not guess."

refutation.rationale: The prompt text in the workflow export matches the quote exactly and includes all the claimed elements: named fields, JSON-only instruction, and the null-not-guess rule.

cards.claim: Candidate built and used twenty synthetic test profiles before recording the demo, including two intentionally broken ones to make sure the exception path actually fires.

citation.quote: I tested the happy path and both exception paths against all twenty profiles before recording the demo.

refutation.rationale: The write-up says twenty profiles were tested before recording, but no test files, test results, or logs are included in the submission. The claim rests entirely on the candidate's word.

cards.claim: The demo shows the exception path running live with a real malformed fixture — jurisdiction is null, validation fails, and the record lands in the exceptions channel with documents attached.

citation.quote: I'll submit the malformed fixture with no jurisdiction. Extraction returns null for jurisdiction because the prompt forbids guessing, validation fails it, and it lands in the exceptions channel with the original documents attached. Nothing silently disappears.

refutation.rationale: The transcript describes the malformed fixture run step by step — null jurisdiction, validation failure, exceptions channel routing — and the workflow export confirms the exceptions path exists to handle exactly this case.

cards.claim: The two malformed test cases were designed to cover specific known failure modes — a missing field and an unreadable contact block — rather than just random bad data.

citation.quote: two of them deliberately malformed (a missing jurisdiction, a contact block pasted as an image description) to exercise the exception path.

refutation.rationale: The write-up names both failure modes (missing jurisdiction, contact block as image description) as deliberate design choices, and the demo shows the missing-jurisdiction case actually firing the exception path.

cards.claim: All demo data is synthetic — candidate hand-authored twenty fake client profiles rather than using any real client PII, and explains this was a deliberate data-handling choice.

citation.quote: Intake documents contain client PII, so the demo runs entirely on twenty synthetic client profiles I authored by hand.

refutation.rationale: The write-up states the profiles were hand-authored synthetics, but no profile files are included in the submission. The data-handling claim is described but not shown.

cards.claim: Candidate chose not to automate conflict screening on principle — treating it as a regulated judgment that must stay with a human — and made this structurally impossible to reach from the automated path.

citation.quote: No automatic conflict screening — that is a regulated judgment I will not automate on principle.

refutation.rationale: The write-up states the principle clearly, and the workflow export has no conflict-screening node — the structural block is real, not just a promise in text.

cards.claim: The workflow's exception path ensures no record ever disappears silently — failures are surfaced with original documents attached so a human can act on them.

citation.quote: Parsing failures and validation misses route to an exceptions channel with the original documents attached, so nothing silently disappears.

refutation.rationale: The exceptions node in the workflow export routes to #onboarding-exceptions with original documents attached, and the demo transcript confirms this path fires on a malformed fixture. Both documents back the claim.

cards.claim: Candidate listed specific things left out, each with a clear reason — OCR was cut because the intake form already produces text and OCR problems would have used up the available time.

citation.quote: No OCR for scanned PDFs — the intake form already produces text, and OCR quality problems would have eaten the timebox.

refutation.rationale: The write-up gives both parts of the reasoning — the intake form already outputs text (making OCR unnecessary) and OCR quality problems would have consumed the available time. The claim accurately reflects the quote.

cards.claim: Candidate named a real, concrete weakness in the current build — the workflow trusts the intake form's entity-type claim more than it should.

citation.quote: The workflow currently trusts the intake form's claim about entity type more than it should.

refutation.rationale: The weakness is named plainly in the write-up. The substance grade is 'asserted,' which is correct — it is a stated concern, not backed by a test case or log showing it causing a problem.

cards.claim: Candidate identified an adoption risk — a noisy exceptions channel would cause coordinators to stop trusting the tool — and described a design decision made to address it.

citation.quote: adoption risk is real: if the exceptions channel gets noisy, coordinators will stop trusting it — so I capped exceptions at two per run and route the rest to a daily digest instead.

refutation.rationale: The write-up says exceptions are capped at two per run with the rest going to a daily digest, but the workflow export shows the daily digest node ('Daily exceptions digest') is a standalone schedule trigger with no incoming connections from the exceptions path — it is not wired up.

cards.claim: Candidate's stated next step — a feedback loop from coordinator corrections into the extraction prompt — follows directly from a named limit in the current build, not a wish list.

citation.quote: With more time I would add a feedback loop from coordinator corrections back into the extraction prompt, because the corrections are the cheapest training data the firm owns.

refutation.rationale: The write-up identifies the limit (the extraction prompt handles current variation but will not learn from corrections) and the next step follows directly from it. The logic is internally consistent.

probes.question: Your write-up says a person checks every extracted profile before it's saved to the CRM. Can you walk me through exactly where that step lives in the workflow — and what happens if the reviewer says no or makes a change?

paragraphs.text: For problem framing (C1), the submission is consistently well-described. The candidate explains why they picked client onboarding intake over the more obvious choice, names a specific cost (25–40 minutes of re-keying per client, errors surfacing weeks later as billing and conflict-check problems), and draws a clear line between what the agent handles and what humans must own. All three cards in this area were assessed as supported. The coordinator feedback behind the time estimate is presented as direct conversation, but no interview notes or other source are included, so the numbers rest on the candidate's account.

For building and execution (C3), the submission is the strongest in the pack. A full n8n workflow export exists with all named nodes connected in the right order, and the extraction prompt is specific enough for someone else to pick up and run. The demo transcript narrates a live end-to-end run — webhook fires, Claude returns a structured profile, CRM record is created, Slack notification appears — but the skeptic notes that a transcript alone cannot confirm the run was live rather than narrated over a staged result. The workflow artifact itself is real and verified; the liveness of the demo is not.

Two evidence cards are directly contradicted by the workflow export, and both are worth probing. First, the write-up says a human reviews every extracted profile before it enters the CRM, but the workflow connects the validation step straight to CRM record creation with no approval or hold node in between (ev-04). Second, the write-up describes a design to cap noisy exceptions and route the rest to a daily digest, but the daily digest node in the export has no incoming connections from the exceptions path — it is not wired up (ev-19). These are not minor gaps; both touch on how the system behaves when something goes wrong or when output quality is uncertain.

For evaluation discipline (C4) and responsible AI (C5), the evidence is partly demonstrated and partly unverified. The exception path firing on a malformed fixture is shown in the demo and confirmed by the workflow structure. The claim that twenty synthetic test profiles were built and run is described but unverifiable — no files or logs were submitted. Similarly, the decision to use hand-authored fake data instead of real client records is stated clearly as a deliberate choice, but no profile files are included to confirm it. The decision to keep conflict screening structurally unreachable from the automated path is backed by the workflow export. On tradeoffs (C6), the candidate names specific cuts with reasons and identifies a real weakness in how the workflow trusts entity-type claims — though no test case or log shows that weakness causing an actual problem.
